paras: The reported lynching at Roanoke, Virginia, was the killing of an unnamed Black man, described as "a colored man," said in a single newspaper brief to have been lynched at Roanoke in July 1888. The brief stated that he had confessed to murdering two women, and it gave no other details of the victim, the lynchers or the killing.

According to the Bossier Banner, a weekly in Bellevue, Louisiana, the man "was lynched last Thursday at Roanoke, Va." Counted from the paper's issue of July 19, "last Thursday" would have been July 12, though the item carried no dateline and the date it was compiled is not shown. The only stated cause was his reported confession to the murder of two women, whose names, like his own, were not printed.
The brief did not say who carried out the lynching, how the man was killed, or whether he had been taken from officers.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and no account of the two killings of women at Roanoke was found.

The Bossier Banner printed the item as one line in its "News Nubs" column, a run of miscellaneous briefs from across the country. It sat between a note on eight locomotives burned at Ashtabula, Ohio, and a report on the Chinese tea crop, with no headline or comment of its own. In the coverage examined, no Virginia paper carried a Roanoke-datelined report of the lynching, so the episode rests on this single out-of-state brief.

Because the brief names no one and has no local confirmation, whether a lynching took place at Roanoke at all, rather than elsewhere in southwestern Virginia that week, cannot be settled from the coverage.

reader.title: Reported lynching at Roanoke, Virginia (July 1888)
bases: The only report says a colored man 'was lynched' at Roanoke after confessing to murdering two women (A10); no other report of the episode was found.

A single one-line brief in a Louisiana weekly says the man was lynched for a confessed double murder (A10), which gives a killing and a pretext of justice, but it names no victim, mob, method or authority, and no Virginia or Roanoke report of the event was found; the brief may be a garbled version of the Wytheville lynching of the same week (A2, A8).

Only the Bossier Banner's brief reports a lynching at Roanoke (A10); Virginia papers of the same week carry a Roanoke column with no lynching (A3) and report a lynching at Wytheville instead (A2, A4).

A Black man (William Henry Smith / Henry Smith / William Jones) charged with assaulting a woman in Pulaski County taken from officers and hanged at Wytheville on the night of 10-11 July; the Roanoke Times reported his wife lived in Roanoke

conflicts.note: The Wytheville reports are about an assault accusation on one woman, not the murder of two, so identity cannot be established; but no Roanoke-datelined lynching was found, the Richmond Dispatch's Roanoke column of 11 July reports none (A3), and the Pulaski case had itself been falsely reported as a lynching on Thursday 5 July (A1, A2, A6).

set_aside: Christiansburg, Va., July 5 brief: a Black man accused of assaulting an old white woman near New River Bridge reported hanged by a mob (a report later contradicted); the Pulaski County episode, not Roanoke.

Wytheville, July 11: William Henry Smith, charged with assaulting a Mrs. Metcalfe of Pulaski County, taken from officers on a train and hanged; notes that papers had reported him lynched the previous Thursday.
Roanoke City column, July 11: Fleming Snead (colored) arrested at Roanoke on a West Virginia murder charge; no lynching.
Virginia News: Henry Smith, accused in the outrage on Mrs. Midhiff of Pulaski County, lynched near Wytheville Tuesday night.
Lynchburg wire: Henry Smith lynched near Wytheville; same Pulaski County episode.
Pulaski County outrage on Mrs. Midkiff: mob of 25 beat the prisoner but did not lynch him; a later Christiansburg rumor said he was hanged and sunk in New River.
Sunday editorial mentions a Black man lynched at Wytheville on Wednesday who was allowed to pray; research called it 'passing', but it is about the Wytheville lynching, not Roanoke.
Quotes the Roanoke Times: the wife of William Jones, hanged by a mob at Wytheville Wednesday night, lives in Roanoke; the only Roanoke link found.
Wytheville, July 12 wire: masked men took William Smith from Sheriff Harkrader and hanged him; says he confessed.
